newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Kuwait set to receive $600 mln for Gulf War oil fires.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait set to receive $600 mln for Gulf War oil fires.

text.p: A Gulf War reparations body was expected to approve a $600 million award to Kuwait Oil Company (KOC) on Monday for the cost of putting out oil well fires started by Iraqi troops, Western diplomats said.
The first corporate claim assessed by the United Nations Compensation Commission (UNCC), the "well blow-out" is of great symbolic importance to the emirate, they added.

At the end of the Gulf War in February 1991, when a coalition of Western and Arab forces led by the United States drove Iraqi troops from Kuwait after a seven-month occupation, 700 oil wells were set alight. They burned for weeks.

A panel of neutral judges, named by the Geneva-based fund, has recommended that KOC be awarded about $600 million of its total $950 million claim for damages filed three years ago, according to diplomats.
The judges, or commissioners, recommended about $350 million should be considered under another claim category, they added.
On Monday the UNCC's Governing Council, composed of representatives from the 15 Security Council member-states, were weighing the judges' report. It is still confidential.
The session was due to end at around 1800 GMT with a final press conference.

"About $600 million has been recommended by the panel of commissioners (judges). They deferred $350 million to go under a different claim and they also rejected a small amount," one Western diplomat told Reuters.
"Our view is that it should go through. It is widely anticipated that the Governing Council will approve the recommendation of the panel," he added.
The arbitrators were Danish, Lebanese and Nigerian.
Some Western diplomats said Iraq had been trying to block the KOC claim from being decided on Monday. In the past, Baghdad has also argued that the fires were a result of Allied bombing.
"Iraq is going all over town complaining that the well-blow claim should be put aside or thrown out," a diplomat said.
Dr. Adel Asem, deputy chairman of Kuwait's Public Authority for assessment of compensation for damages resulting from the Iraqi aggression, was to address the closed-door meeting.

Abdul Rahman Al-Houty, former chairman of Kuwait's Public Authority, in a statement in December 1994 to the Governing Council, referred to the KOC claim as "the most notorious and injurious of all the many direct losses suffered as a result of Iraq's unlawful invasion and occupation of Kuwait".
It was not immediately known whether an Iraqi representative was attending the Governing Council, but Baghdad has made a request to take part, according to a U.N. statement.
Iraqi deputy foreign minister Riyadh al-Qaysi lobbied the Governing Council last July to set aside money to mount a legal defence against claims, saying the embargo deprived it of funds.

During oral hearings on the case, Qaysi also asked that consideration of the well-blow claim be suspended to give Baghdad more time to prepare its case. But the panel rejected the bid, prompting the Iraqi delegation to walk out.

The UNCC, set up by the Security Council in 1991 to assess claims from individuals, firms, and governments for direct lossess caused by Iraq's invasion and occupation, has received claims totalling $200 billion.
But its funding, so far dependent on government donations and seized Iraqi assets, has been precarious.

The fund has been buoyed by recent implementation of the oil-for-food deal between the United Nations and Iraq. Under the six-month renewable deal, the UNCC is to receive 30 per cent of oil export revenues -- meaning about $100 million a month.
U.N. officials said last week that UNCC's share of revenues should enable it to begin paying substantial reparations to individual claimants by March.
To date, it has only been able to pay out $13.4 million in awards to 4,000 priority claimants for death of a close relative or serious personal injury.
